# Screws That Fit Nothing

My father labeled everything. I knew this the way you know the weather of the house you grew up in, but I didn't understand it until the week after the funeral, when I opened the door to his workshop and found forty years of masking tape looking back at me.

*Washers, small.* *Washers, smaller.* *Hinges (good).* *Hinges (someday).* The handwriting was all capitals, blocky and slanted slightly left, the same hand that had signed my report cards and written *DRIVE SAFE* on the back of every envelope he ever mailed me, as though the post office might deliver the warning faster than I could get into a car.

My brother said we should hire someone. There are people, apparently, who come and clear out the houses of the dead. They sort, they haul, they sell what can be sold and throw away the rest, and you never have to touch any of it. He sent me a link. The company's logo was a sun rising over a clean horizon, which struck me as either very kind or very cruel.

I told him I'd do the workshop myself. He didn't argue. He'd never liked that room. It smelled of sawdust and machine oil and something sharper underneath, a scorched smell from the time in 1994 when Dad tried to fix the toaster and the toaster won. My brother associated the room with being asked to hold things. Hold this steady. Hold this light. No, *here*. I associated it with the same thing, but I'd liked it. There's a particular trust in being asked to hold the light. It means someone believes you'll keep it where it needs to be.

So I started on a Saturday with a roll of contractor bags and a thermos of coffee and every intention of being ruthless.

I lasted about twenty minutes.

The problem wasn't sentiment, exactly. The problem was that everything had been *decided*. My father had already looked at every object in that room and determined what it was and what it was for. Throwing something away meant overruling him, and I found I couldn't do it casually. A coffee can marked *Nails, bent, straighten later* was not trash. It was a promise he'd made to himself, and the fact that he'd never kept it didn't make it less of one.

I began making piles instead. Keep. Donate. Brother. Undecided. Undecided grew fastest.

Around noon I found the jar.

It was on the highest shelf, behind a row of paint cans so old their labels had faded to the color of weak tea. A pickle jar, the big kind, full nearly to the lid with screws. Brass and steel, flat-head and Phillips, long and stubby, some with threads so fine they looked etched, some so coarse they could have held a boat together. On the lid, in the familiar capitals:

*SCREWS THAT FIT NOTHING.*

I sat down on his stool and laughed until I had to put the jar on the floor.

Because of course. Of course he had kept them. Every time he'd taken something apart and found a screw left over, every time he'd bought a pack of twenty and used nineteen, every time a mystery screw had turned up in a drawer or a pocket or the lint trap of the dryer, he had tried it against every hole he could find, and when it fit none of them, he hadn't thrown it away. He'd put it here. And then he'd labeled the jar, which meant he'd known. He'd understood exactly what he was doing. This wasn't a jar of screws waiting to be sorted. This was a jar of screws that had been sorted, thoroughly and finally, into the category of *useless*, and kept anyway.

I thought about what my mother would have said. She'd died eleven years before him, and she had been a thrower-out, a clearer of surfaces, a woman who believed that anything you hadn't touched in a year was simply taking up the space where something better might go. They'd fought about the workshop for as long as I could remember. Not cruelly. It was the kind of argument that becomes a sort of song a couple sings together, the same verses every time. *What are you keeping that for?* *You never know.* *I do know. I know you'll never use it.* *Then I'll never use it here, where it's not bothering anybody.*

I unscrewed the lid and poured a handful into my palm. They were cold and heavier than I expected. A few were rusted. One was bright gold, tiny, the kind that holds the arm of a pair of glasses. I wondered whose glasses. I wondered if they'd been mine.

Here's what I think now, though I didn't think it all at once.

I think my father knew perfectly well that most things in the world don't fit. That you spend your life with pieces left over: conversations that never found their place, apologies that arrived after the hole they were meant for had closed up, love shaped wrong for whatever it was aimed at. And I think he decided, in his quiet, capital-lettered way, that not fitting wasn't the same as not mattering. That a thing could be useless and still be worth keeping. That you could look at something clearly, name it honestly, *this fits nothing*, and still put it on the high shelf where it would be safe.

I didn't hire the people with the sunrise logo. I did, eventually, get ruthless. The bent nails went. The paint cans went. Most of the hinges, good and someday, went to a man from the church who builds cabinets for families who've lost their houses to fire.

But the jar is on a shelf in my kitchen now, between the flour and the good olive oil. My daughter asked me what it was for, and I told her the truth: nothing. She considered this with the seriousness of a seven-year-old and asked if she could add to it.

Last week she brought me a screw she'd found on the sidewalk outside school. We tried it in everything, the cabinet doors, the back of the radio, the battery panel of her flashlight. It didn't fit.

She held the jar steady while I dropped it in.
